body:
Thank you for your contribution!

This is a pretty majorly breaking change, is there a proposal to track this or to evaluate support?

This would benefit from having a proper proposal created [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals) to discuss the details and evaluate support for this, as it would be something that would need good support to justify the changes and the need for them

I'd say backwards compatibility needs to be maintained by creating new methods instead of replacing the existing ones, as this would be very disruptive to anyone using the existing interfaces

This is a very valuable pull request, however I share @AThousandShips's concerns about compatibility breakage. This would not only create extra work for users when updating Godot versions, but it would make it very difficult to write plugins that support multiple engine versions simultaneously.

To align on the direction, it would be great if you could respond to the high-level concerns before changing implementation details. Please also note that every push notifies 4 reviewer teams. Thanks! :slightly_smiling_face:

> Thank you for your contribution!
> 
> This is a pretty majorly breaking change, is there a proposal to track this or to evaluate support?
> 
> This would benefit from having a proper proposal created [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals) to discuss the details and evaluate support for this, as it would be something that would need good support to justify the changes and the need for them
> 
> I'd say backwards compatibility needs to be maintained by creating new methods instead of replacing the existing ones, as this would be very disruptive to anyone using the existing interfaces

> This is a very valuable pull request, however I share @AThousandShips's concerns about compatibility breakage. This would not only create extra work for users when updating Godot versions, but it would make it very difficult to write plugins that support multiple engine versions simultaneously.
> 
> To align on the direction, it would be great if you could respond to the high-level concerns before changing implementation details. Please also note that every push notifies 4 reviewer teams. Thanks! 🙂

Thanks for the feedback.

I agree this is a significant breaking change, and I understand the concerns around backward compatibility and plugin support. This PR was intended to demonstrate a redesigned API focused on performance and type safety, not to incrementally extend the existing one while keeping compatibility.

Since this direction would need a proposal and broader consensus first, and maintaining parallel APIs is outside what I can commit to right now, I will close this PR in its current form. If anyone wants to follow up with a proposal or continue the discussion, it can always be reopened.

Apologies for spamming the notifications with all the pushes 😅

In light of the recent discussions and the [proposal](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/15215) provided by @Chestnut45, I've completely changed the approach to address the previous compatibility concerns.

Instead of replacing the existing methods and breaking backward compatibility, this PR now adds new, non-allocating, typed variants alongside the original ones. I have updated the PR description with the new details and force-pushed the updated implementation.

Let me know what you think of the new direction!

Please note that we no longer accept feature PRs from new contributors, see [here](https://godotengine.org/article/contribution-policy-2026/)

Given the large scope of this PR and that it is breaking compatibility I think this will unfortunately be closed again due to this

> Given the large scope of this PR and that it is breaking compatibility I think this will unfortunately be closed again due to this

I understand the concern, but just to clarify, I have specifically refactored this PR to ensure it is backward-compatible, so it does not break existing code.
That's good, the scale is still concerning from a new contributor though, but I'll let the relevant teams decide

I want to put my 2 cents in now that I've had a chance to read over the new implementation. This is the perfect solution. I understand and agree that it's important to vet large PRs, especially from new contributors, but *please* don't let a gem like this fall through the cracks without a careful review first just because it's a feature PR (It's arguable that this is even a "new" feature, since much of the current API was only meant to be a temporary solution until a better method was found).

Under the guidelines I believe I'm also considered a new contributor, but I do have a degree in computer science with a specialization in video game programming, and would be more than happy to contribute to any formalized review process if the motivation isn't there for current maintainers.
It may be ideal to encourage discussions on this PR on [RocketChat](https://chat.godotengine.org/channel/general), possibly in the [#physics](https://chat.godotengine.org/channel/physics) channel.

I wonder if the `.collision_count` and `.max_collisions` properties of `PhysicsPointIntersectionResult2D`/`3D` and `PhysicsShapeIntersectionResult2D`/`3D` should instead be named `.intersection_count` and `.max_intersections`. Likewise, the `collision_index` parameter of their methods could be renamed to `intersection_index`. 

Initially, I chose these names for consistency with `PhysicsShapeCollisionResult2D`/`3D`, but I now think consistency should instead follow the methods that produce these results `intersect_point_into()` and `intersect_shape_into()`

I think the internal consistency of the new result types' properties following the methods for naming like that is a good idea and is unambiguous, but it may be simpler (and more in line with the current API) to use `max_results`, `result_count`, and `result_index` for all of them, to mirror what the current query methods use for wording.

I have no strong feelings either way though, and think both are perfectly acceptable. Whatever is preferred by maintainers :)

Linking the small discussion that was had in RocketChat here so it's easier to find for reviewers: <https://chat.godotengine.org/channel/physics/thread/6WEXTx24Rdt6LijTv>

Towards the end of the thread I explain why structs / custom variants are necessarily worse solutions, since they would still require per-query allocations even if we had those features today, unlike this PR.

As well, please don't be put off by the +2,000 lines. It's mostly just documentation and class boilerplate for the new result types and methods, and there isn't even any new logic to review.

This should be a slam dunk; It benefits all users, there's no downsides, and it solves the problem at the source without adding any complexity.

Thanks very much for taking the time to review this!

I agree with your points about the naming and the edge case in setting the maximum number of results. As well, I don't see any harm in changing the read-only `result_count` properties to `count()` and `max_results` to `resize(max_results)` and `size()` if that style is preferred.

I don't think changes which misalign the new API with the existing one such as multiple results from ray queries or unification of the shape queries should be in the scope of this PR. I would argue that it's more important to fix the current performance and type-safety issues without changing the existing API rather than a full rewrite, which might be better suited for a future major release instead. Having the new methods differ in functionality from the current ones would likely lead to confusion as to why they're named as suffixed versions of the existing methods in the first place, and would make this PR more complex than it needs to be imo.

Thanks for the review.

Regarding the `_no_alloc` suffix, I agree that `_typed` is redundant because the type is already in the signature. However, I feel `_no_alloc` suffers from the same redundancy. Since the user is required to pass in their own pre-allocated result object as a parameter, the signature already implies that the engine isn't allocating a new container.

The reason I went with the singular `Result2D`/`3D` (and `get_collision_count()`) is to stay strictly consistent with established classes like `PhysicsTestMotionResult2D`/`3D`, even though a test motion can yield multiple contacts.

That being said, I completely agree with you that the term "collision" doesn't make sense for point intersections. This is why I previously proposed changing them to `.intersection_count` (`.get_intersection_count()`) and `.max_intersections` (`.set_max_intersections(...)`) for `PhysicsPointIntersectionResult2D`/`3D` and `PhysicsShapeIntersectionResult2D`/`3D`. This fixes the terminology while staying consistent with the established naming convention of `PhysicsTestMotionResult2D`/`3D::get_collision_count()`.

If there is still a strong consensus in favor of `_no_alloc`, `Results2D`/`3D`, `count()`, and `resize(...)`, I am willing to make the changes.

> I don't think changes which misalign the new API with the existing one such as multiple results from ray queries or unification of the shape queries should be in the scope of this PR. (...) Having the new methods differ in functionality from the current ones would likely lead to confusion as to why they're named as suffixed versions of the existing methods in the first place (...)

Those are good points. (Multiple results from ray queries could be done while keeping the default of 1 result at most, and with a default value of `0` for `result_index` parameters, as in `PhysicsTestMotionResult2D`/`3D`, to keep a compatible API. Now that I mention this, I suppose this can be done later without breaking compatibility.)

> Regarding the `_no_alloc` suffix, I agree that _typed is redundant because the type is already in the signature. However, I feel `_no_alloc` suffers from the same redundancy. Since the user is required to pass in their own pre-allocated result object as a parameter, the signature already implies that the engine isn't allocating a new container.

Having a result object in the method signature by itself doesn't guarantee that no more allocations are done. I still prefer the `_no_alloc` suffix, because I find it more informative and telling users something more important and interesting. Also I just find the `_typed` suffix very ugly, personally.

> The reason I went with the singular `Result2D`/`3D` (and `get_collision_count()`) is to stay strictly consistent with established classes like `PhysicsTestMotionResult2D`/`3D`, even though a test motion can yield multiple contacts.

That is fair. I won't insist on using `Results` instead of `Result`. This then makes me lean a bit more strongly toward replacing `max_results` though. Also, to be really consistent with `PhysicsTestMotionResult2D`/`3D` you should have only getters, and not read-only properties. (Note read-only properties could be added later, and then also cover `PhysicsTestMotionResult2D`/`3D`, if at all.)

This is also making me think that perhaps better class names would be those derived directly from the method names, namely `PhysicsCastMotionResult` (no change), `PhysicsIntersectPointResult`, `PhysicsIntersectRayResult`, `PhysicsGetRestInfoResult`, `PhysicsCollideShapeResult`, `PhysicsIntersectShapeResult`. This way you can guess them very easily from the method name. (Note even in the current state of this PR, the result class names are already deviating from the parameter class names.) Some of those names are mildly ugly, but we could do this intentionally to keep prettier names available for future improved APIs (in 4.x, without breaking compatibility). What do you think?

> That being said, I completely agree with you that the term "collision" doesn't make sense for point intersections. This is why I previously proposed changing them to `.intersection_count` (`.get_intersection_count()`) and `.max_intersections` (`.set_max_intersections(...)`) for `PhysicsPointIntersectionResult2D`/`3D` and `PhysicsShapeIntersectionResult2D`/`3D`. This fixes the terminology while staying consistent with the established naming convention of `PhysicsTestMotionResult2D/3D::get_collision_count()`.

Fair point. I forgot `PhysicsTestMotionResult3D.get_collision_count` was already named that way (there is no such function in `PhysicsTestMotionResult2D` though). I guess using `max_intersections` and `get_intersection_count()` for the intersection queries could be fine too. The main reason for consistent naming (for me) is to make it easier to swap them out in code, and I guess it would be more likely that you replace an intersection query by another intersection query anyway. This naming is also another way of avoiding the clash of `Result` with `max_results`.

I do think using getters instead of read-only properties would be the conservative way to go here, even though it will cause some extra typing (ha) for users. This would also single out the `max_intersections` (etc.) property in the documentation (because properties have their own section before methods), as the only thing you can set, which I think would be good.

> Someone brought up that the `_no_alloc` methods could still allocate internally, and probably do in some cases. (...) It could be argued that that should be done before merging this PR, but personally I do not mind leaving it as a follow-up.

I agree that making the methods fully allocation-free internally would be another improvement worth doing in the future, though I have a stronger stance personally that such an improvement should *not* be required before merging this PR. In my view the internal allocations are a different (albeit closely related) issue, and I don't see any real benefit to holding off on merging this in the meantime, especially given how substantial the speedups already are using this new API over the current one.

I'd be curious to see what the conditions are for seeing those internal allocations and how much impact eliminating them will have on top of this, though I would imagine the performance increase won't be nearly as impactful. I can't say I'd be unhappy to be proven wrong, though!

On the name, I think `_inplace` as 1 word is perfectly fine.
There's a precedent in the standard library ([`inplace_merge`](https://cppreference.com/cpp/algorithm/inplace_merge), [`inplace_vector`](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/container/inplace_vector)).

>     1. Passing in an object to be written into is a bit unorthodox for the Godot API in general, and could be confusing. However, it seems there's precedence for this with `NavigationServer*D.query_path` already, so that arguably makes that point moot. (**EDIT:** I totally forgot about `PhysicsServer*D.body_test_motion` as well, which was obviously mentioned in the PR description)

Doing it any other way would require allocating a result object, which defeats the main benefit of this PR.

>     2. I didn't like the `_typed` suffix, and I frankly don't like the new `_no_alloc` suffix either, but more on that below.

I agree with your points, and would like to suggest (in order of current preference): `_buffered` rather than `_buffer`, or `_inplace` like was suggested by @Bromeon . The more I think about it, `_into` is a fine suffix as well, though I didn't like it at first due to the spatial ambiguity you mentioned. Honestly I wouldn't be bothered by any of these 3, and agree they're all at least better than `_typed` and `_no_alloc`. 

>     3. Having both variants sit alongside eachother, potentially confusing people. Granted, the query API isn't very approachable to begin with, but that also isn't an argument for making it more confusing.

Again, there's no other option without breaking compatibility, which was rejected. I don't think it's worth letting the current API (which is unacceptably slow and quite clunky) remain for any longer just because it's a bit ugly (granted) to have multiple versions of the query methods next to each other.
Can we ditch the `Dictionary` result type?

> Can we ditch the `Dictionary` result type?

Probably not until after version 5.0. Usually, a major version is when you can break compatibility, but I'm not completely sure if that's how Godot handles it or if they're planning to get rid of container results altogether.

If you look at the history of this PR, it originally attempted to replace the current methods. However, compatibility concerns were raised, so it now tries to add these methods on top of the existing ones.

I notice you've requested a review from me, but I'm certain I'm still too new to contributing for that to make a difference (and I'm not sure I'm supposed to until I've contributed more), so I won't add an official review unless requested by another maintainer :sweat_smile: 

From what I understand, you've addressed all of @mihe 's concerns locally and are waiting for feedback on 2 things before pushing:

- The `cast_motion` behaviour either matching the existing implementation exactly by returning false only for errors (still returning true when no collision occurs), or becoming consistent with all other query methods by returning true only when a collision is detected. I feel the current behaviour is worse UX, and would argue for returning true only when a collision occurs, but I completely understand if strict adherence to the current implementations is more important than a small UX improvement for the new suffixed methods, so that users aren't confused by an implementation difference between a variant of a method that's supposed to have the same functionality as the original.
- Consensus on the suffix. After much thought I believe either `_into` or `_buffered` would be best. `_into` is short and idiomatic, but may cause some confusion and doesn't capture the benefits of pre allocation. `_buffered` I think captures the benefits nicely, doesn't promise exactly zero allocation, and doesn't have the same problem of seemingly referring to a raw chunk of memory like `_buffer` does, but may still be confusing to some.

I'm curious to see what everyone thinks, though I hope we can come to consesnsus soon so this can be merged before 4.8 feature freeze :) It'd be a shame to miss that deadline just for trying to find a "perfect" name.
Just as a heads up, it might be a few more days before I get around to doing a second pass on this and respond to some of the unresolved issues/comments here.

>    `_into` has some precedence in popular languages/APIs as well, with largely the exact same purpose as what we're doing here, like Python's [`socket.recv_into`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/socket.html#socket.socket.recv_into), Kotlin's [`*Array.copyInto`](https://kotlinlang.org/api/core/kotlin-stdlib/kotlin.collections/copy-into.html), the web's [`TextEncoder.encodeInto`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/TextEncoder/encodeInto), and I'm sure many more. But again, the spatial ambiguity is not ideal.

A less spatially ambiguous option for method names here is `try_intersect_ray` since these all return `bool` indicating whether a result was found. This is a common method name pattern in C# at least, and it's been used at least once already in Godot's `Mutex` with `try_lock`.

>     Thinking about `_in_place`/`_inplace` some more, especially given how C++ uses it, might in fact make it less fitting, since it's more about placement construction given some set of parameters, rather than filling an out-parameter, but maybe I'm nitpicking.

I now agree, in terms of potentially misleading implications from the naming this is probably not the best option.

>     `_buffered` to me is something very different from `_buffer`, making me think of buffered input or I/O in general, as in you're storing a series of something for some kind of deferral.

Granted for the same reason.

> My vote is still on `_into`, but I'd like to see some other maintainers sign off on it as well.

Even with the spatial ambiguity, I agree that this is the best option. Even though it may be a bit confusing, I'd argue it's not really *misleading* in the same way as the other suggestions so far due to the signatures themselves remaining largely the same as the established methods, and not aligning with the potential misinterpretation the name might initially suggest to some. The precedence argument adds weight to this too, I haven't seen `_into` used to mean anything other than what we're doing here in other languages before, and it is used quite frequently.

Not a maintainer but I am now firmly in camp `_into` as well.

As for `try_` as a prefix... I have to admit it doesn't have the same ambiguity, and does fit quite well with the return values for most of these methods. I personally don't like it as much mainly because it sounds like (to me at least) it can fail for other reasons than the query not having any results. `try_get_rest_info` in particular I feel would be the worst offender. Even with 0 resting contacts, the query still succeeded.
I'm on board with the `_into` naming, and the current proposed API looks fine to me.

One more point to bring up, I questioned it on RC:

The new API (mirroring the old) assumes 1 result for e.g. ray tests (closest?). This works currently but there's some significant likelihood we will want to be able to do tests reporting multiple results in the future.

We don't want to to close this off, and we ideally don't want to e.g. end up in a situation where we have 2 versions of each result structure, one for single hits and one for multiple. So it might be worth thinking in advance how we can deal with both at the same time (or with the least problems stored up for the future).

I totally agree that we should avoid having two versions of the result objects, but I think for now we should closely follow the default methods to maintain backward compatibility while improving performance, at least until we reach a major version.

> I totally agree that we should avoid having two versions of the result objects, but I think for now we should closely follow the default methods to maintain backward compatibility while improving performance, at least until we reach a major version.

I second this. If you want multiple results from a raycast, it's already very easy to do so with a shape intersection or multiple chained raycasts, which when using this new API would also not require allocation per-raycast anymore.

I think such a feature is definitely out of scope for this PR and should not block it.

That being said, for the future, I agree adding the default argument for the result index is the best option, but it was shot down earlier in this discussion, so the other methods (e.g. `PhysicsCollideShapeResult[2|3]D`) do not have default values for the result index parameters anymore.

If we're dead-set on not having index = 0 (which I really don't understand there being a problem with), another option is to have the multi-raycast functionality added as a separate method that writes into a passed Array of the current single result objects rather than making a new result object. This has precedent in for instance Unity with Physics.RaycastAll, though it would require the user to ensure none of the array elements are null, which could be a potential source of confusion.

Since there are 2 obvious ways to fix this later without breaking compat (and it's not exactly a hotly-needed feature and has current workarounds), I personally feel it's not really worth discussing further here.

> We don't want to to close this off, and we ideally don't want to e.g. end up in a situation where we have 2 versions of each result structure, one for single hits and one for multiple. So it might be worth thinking in advance how we can deal with both at the same time (or with the least problems stored up for the future).

My stance on this is that the moment we turn this PR into "let's fix and/or futureproof the API while we're at it" it loses all meaning and _should_ rightfully balloon in scope to such a degree that it should just be closed outright in favor of a full API revamp (that may or may not happen).

To be clear, I think that's a perfectly defensible way to go with this, but let's at least be honest with ourselves about what we want, instead of ending up with some half-and-half solution of adding a couple of default parameters here and there. I'd rather not see these new methods become "the new API" and start diverging from the old, even we did dip our toes a little bit with the `collider` changes, but that was arguably buggy behavior anyway.

In my mind these new methods and their respective result objects are just a different form of calling the old API, and would be deprecated in their entirety along with the old API if/when somebody takes a crack at redesigning the physics query API as a whole (which is arguably needed).

> I second this. If you want multiple results from a raycast, it's already very easy to do so with a shape intersection or multiple chained raycasts, which when using this new API would also not require allocation per-raycast anymore.

Yeah but this is super inefficient from a ray casting point of view when you can do it all at once if you want multiple hits. It also exposes special cases, like you have the first object hit, you want to cast from there onwards, so you now have to introduce an exception so that it won't register a _second_ hit with the first object etc etc.

> I think such a feature is definitely out of scope for this PR and should not block it.

Just to be clear, I'm absolutely not suggesting to add multi-hit ray casting in this PR, or significantly alter the API. It's more that if there's one thing we have learned about adding API, it's to think of the future. c++ wise we don't always over future-proof (indeed Juan was not a fan of over doing this and there are some docs about it), but API wise at least it can be an absolute pain if we don't at least _consider_ a little of future cases and leave the door open where we can. We can easily end up in a situation with 10 different versions of an API function etc, all doing the same thing slightly differently. :grin: 

> That being said, for the future, I agree adding the default argument for the result index is the best option, but it was shot down earlier in this discussion, so the other methods (e.g. PhysicsCollideShapeResult[2|3]D) do not have default values for the result index parameters anymore.

It's not necessary to add a default argument in this PR (that functionality doesn't exist yet), it's more can we add this in future without breaking compat. I'm pretty sure it should be fine, as default arguments are a common way to introduce new parameters, but worth mentioning at this stage in case anyone sees any snags in this.

> In my mind these new methods and their respective result objects are just a different form of calling the old API, and would be deprecated in their entirety along with the old API if/when somebody takes a crack at redesigning the physics query API as a whole (which is arguably needed).

I'm on board with this interpretation, especially if that means this can be merged as is.

I would be very happy to participate in a full redesign aimed at 5.0, but I do think this is absolutely worth having in the meantime for performance reasons alone.

> Yeah but this is super inefficient from a ray casting point of view when you can do it all at once if you want multiple hits.

For the chained raycasts, I agree it's not nearly as efficient and was perhaps a poor suggestion on my part.

The shape intersection workaround is not super inefficient though, and I feel like it's much better suited for the kind of query you're describing ("give me all of the objects that intersect this shape"), rather than a multi-hit raycast which I would expect to still potentially hit objects multiple times, since each hit has unique and useful contact information like position, normal, etc.

> It also exposes special cases, like you have the first object hit, you want to cast from there onwards, so you now have to introduce an exception so that it won't register a _second_ hit with the first object etc etc.

I don't think that's the case. Ray casting from inside an object doesn't detect it unless `hit_from_inside` is true in the query parameters, which is false by default. Obviously this doesn't prevent multiple hits on concave shapes where the ray can exit and then reenter the shape, but again I really think we should expect those additional hits to be reported in a multi-hit raycast anyway (or at least configurable as an option like `ignore_duplicates`), otherwise it becomes much more than a simple raycast operation and begins having an opinion about what kind of hits it should care about.

> It's not necessary to add a default argument in this PR (that functionality doesn't exist yet) ...

Of course, I meant for queries like shape collisions which already return multiple results. They used to (in an earlier version of this PR) have default arguments for the result indices in the accessor methods, though I suppose that's a different situation and there's not actually a practical reason for those to have defaults, unlike the case with adding multiple results to raycasts (though I still agree with mihe that something like that should probably be part of a complete redesign rather than tacked-on to this, even later).
Adding a default argument (with the necessary compatibility methods) would be fine indeed!

Just to keep this up to date:

In core on RC there's just a last minute wobble on whether we should go with multiple result classes (as in this PR), or consolidate them further. Will update once consensus has been reached.

Sorry about the small delay.

There were some concerns about the PR introducing 12 classes for each individual result, and the resulting class / docs / engine bloat.

## Trade-offs
It would be possible to consolidate these result classes, for instance into `PhysicsResult3D` and `PhysicsResult2D`, or some other simple scheme. These were some of the main upsides / downsides we discussed (not exhaustive).

### Upsides _(of consolidation)_
* Fewer new `ClassDB` classes introduced
* Easier to expand with new physics queries, or multi-hit tests, without requiring yet _more_ classes

### Downsides _(of consolidation)_
* Doesn't work as well with the existing editor auto-complete
* Greater possibility of confusing users

We discussed this extensively on RC, in core channels, and in discussion threads, as well as with the TLC (not at a formal meeting, since the next one isn't scheduled until after feature freeze, but we did have an active thread).

@Ivorforce, who is familiar with ClassDB, confirmed that technically the memory/performance cost of the added classes is unlikely to be very high. Therefore, the argument either way seems to mostly come down to UX: cleaner documentation, fewer classes to browse, and avoiding future confusion should we decide to introduce a _third_ API or deprecate this one.

Most of those involved in reviewing the original PR/proposal seemed keen for it to go ahead in its current form. I'm personally happy either way - I see pros and cons to both approaches - and if most people prefer the multi-class approach, we should go for it. @clayjohn has also expressed that he is fine with this going ahead despite the investigation into alternative approaches.
Looks like the issue is now resolved; preparing the merge batch as we speak!
Thanks! Congratulations on your first merged contribution! 🎉
